title: Historically Informed Performance
scope: Flute and keyboard (harpsichord, clavichord, piano). L. Mozart's violin treatise is used only as a cross-reference: bowing ↔ flute breath/tonguing ↔ keyboard touch.

sources.title: On Playing the Flute (Versuch einer Anweisung die Flöte traversiere zu spielen, 1752)
sources.note: Flute treatise that is also a general guide to performance, ensemble playing and the keyboard accompanist (Ch. XVII sec. VI).

sources.title: Essay on the True Art of Playing Keyboard Instruments (1753/1762)
sources.note: The keyboard counterpart to Quantz; both worked at Frederick II's court in Berlin and disagree on several points.

sources.title: Interpreting Bach at the Keyboard
sources.note: Applies the 18th-century sources to J. S. Bach on harpsichord and piano.

sources.title: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
sources.note: Instrument choice, tempo groups, articulation and dynamics in Bach.

sources.title: A Treatise on the Fundamental Principles of Violin Playing (1756)
sources.note: Used only to cross-check and to map bowing onto flute breath/tonguing and keyboard touch.

groups.title: Foundations
groups.blurb: What "good execution" meant to these authors: the orator analogy, affect, and the faults to avoid.

groups.title: Tempo
groups.blurb: Quantz's pulse system, Bodky's tempo groups, and how to choose a tempo from the notes themselves.

groups.title: Rhythm
groups.blurb: Dotted notes, Lombard rhythm, unequal quick notes, dotted notes against triplets, rests and rubato.

groups.title: Articulation & breathing
groups.blurb: Flute tonguing and breathing, keyboard touch, and the bowing analogy that links them.

groups.title: Ornaments
groups.blurb: Appoggiaturas, trills, small graces, how much to ornament, and cadenzas.

groups.title: Dynamics
groups.blurb: Light and shade, dissonance-based dynamics, messa di voce, and what each keyboard can do.

groups.title: Instruments
groups.blurb: Flute specifics; harpsichord, clavichord and piano; choosing an instrument for Bach.

groups.title: Accompanying & ensemble
groups.blurb: The keyboard as timekeeper, accompanying a soloist, and rubato over a steady bass.

groups.title: Where the sources disagree
groups.blurb: A single table of the points on which Quantz, C. P. E. Bach, L. Mozart and the modern authors differ.

topics.title: Good execution: the orator analogy
topics.summary: Quantz compares the performer to an orator: the same speech, or piece, can move or bore depending on delivery. Execution is half the work; a mediocre piece well played beats a good piece badly played.

rules.text: Execution must be true and distinct: every note heard, in tune, articulated as marked.
It must be rounded and complete: each note gets its true value; the tempo is kept.
It must be easy and flowing: no visible effort, no grimaces.
It must be varied: light and shade, a constant alternation of piano and forte.
It must be expressive: fitted to each passion, which may change from phrase to phrase.

guidelines.text: Separate ideas that do not belong together even where there is no rest, especially when one phrase ends and the next begins on the same pitch.
Learn to play well in an ensemble part before playing solos; L. Mozart says the same for violinists.
"Play from the soul, not like a trained bird": you can only move listeners if you are moved yourself.

terms.def: Execution, delivery: the manner of performance (Quantz's key term).
The emotional character a passage expresses; the performer must identify and convey it.

topics.title: Reading the affect from the notes
topics.summary: Quantz gives four clues to the dominant sentiment of a piece. They decide tempo, articulation, ornaments and dynamics.

guidelines.text: In most pieces the passion changes; adopt a new sentiment almost bar by bar.
A temperament that is too hot should cool itself in the Adagio; a melancholy one should borrow fire for the Allegro.

steps: Mode: major usually gay, bold, serious or sublime; minor usually flattering, melancholy or tender (with exceptions).

Intervals and articulation: slurred close intervals → flattering, sad, tender; short detached notes and wide leaps → gay, bold; dotted and sustained notes → serious, pathetic; long notes mixed with quick ones → majestic.
Dissonances: their kind and density (see Dissonance dynamics).
The tempo word: Allegro, Affettuoso, Mesto… which also names a character, not just a speed.

topics.title: Checklist: faults of poor execution
topics.summary: Quantz closes his chapter with a list of faults. It works as a self-review checklist after recording yourself.
steps: Out of tune, forced tone.
Indistinct, unarticulated, sluggish or dry notes; everything slurred, or everything attacked the same way.
Tempo not kept; notes not given their value.
Adagio graces too long or against the harmony; graces badly finished or rushed; dissonances not resolved.
Passage-work heavy, anxious or blundering; grimaces.
Everything at one level, no piano and forte; contradicting the affect; playing "on commission" without feeling.
Keyboard: notes held too long ("sticky") or let go "as if the keys burned"; hacking and thumping.

topics.title: Quantz's pulse system
topics.summary: Quantz uses a healthy pulse of about 80 beats per minute as a pocket metronome and sorts tempo words into four classes, each twice as slow as the one before.

rules.text: Common time: Allegro assai = one pulse per minim; Allegretto = per crotchet; Adagio cantabile = per quaver; Adagio assai = two pulses per quaver.
Alla breve (¢): every value is taken twice as fast as in common time.
A plain "Allegro" (also Poco allegro, Vivace) sits between the first two classes: one pulse per three quavers.
No more than eight very fast notes fit in one pulse, whether double-tongued or bowed: the fastest notes in the piece limit the tempo.

guidelines.text: Set the Allegro by its hardest passage so you never have to slow down for it.
Treat the classes as a guide, not a law: C. P. E. Bach says Berlin played adagios slower and allegros faster than elsewhere.
A repeated fast piece may be taken a little faster the second time.
Arias and church music: somewhat more moderate than instrumental pieces.

Adagio pesante, Lento, Largo assai, Mesto, Grave
tables.note: Plain Allegro: crotchet ≈ 120. Metronome equivalents follow Reilly's note (p. 286).

topics.title: Bodky's tempo groups for Bach
topics.summary: Bodky argues that Bach's tempos fall into a small number of groups tied to affect and rhythmic organisation, and proposes five, centred on the heartbeat.

guidelines.text: The same inner beat can run across different time signatures.
Metre and note values alone do not fix the tempo: Bach notated the same piece in different metres.

tables.title: Five groups
columns: Approx. MM of the inner beat
tables.note: 80 ≈ heartbeat, the pivot. The upper limit reflects the historical harpsichord action. Bodky admits the scheme rests on internal evidence.

checks: Compared with Quantz's four classes: both pivot on ≈80.
flags: Bodky's figures are his own hypothesis, not an 18th-century rule.

topics.title: Choosing a tempo for Bach
topics.summary: Bach rarely marked tempos. Badura-Skoda and Bodky reconstruct them from metre, note values, dance type and character.

guidelines.text: 18th-century tempos were generally faster and lighter than many 20th-century habits.
Little ritardando except in toccatas, fantasias and recitatives; final ritardandos smaller than today.
Allegros not rushed, adagios not dragged: the general content and the quickest notes decide.

steps: Identify the dance or the kind of motion (some fugues are gigue-like; chorale preludes may be in dance style).
Find the fastest notes and the hardest passage; the tempo must let them sound clearly.
Check the metre: alla breve and compound metres change the counting unit (Quantz tables).
Choose a beat you can keep steady: strict time was a chief virtue (Muffat, Quantz; Bach's own conducting described as fast and very steady).
Let slow movements be "in one breath" rather than too slow.

topics.title: Dotted notes and over-dotting
topics.summary: All three primary sources shorten the note after a dot in lively or majestic music. Quantz applies it to dotted quavers and shorter values.

rules.text: After a dotted quaver (or shorter), the short note is as short as the shortest notes in the piece, whatever the tempo; the dot is lengthened.
Short notes after dots are always shorter than written; four or more short notes after a dot are played rapidly.

guidelines.text: Long dots in slow, tender music sound more flattering; sharp dots with very short notes sound majestic.
In rapid tempos a long succession of dots may be played almost as rests; dots after long notes or in slow tempos are held.
French overtures (Partita 4, the Overture in the French Manner, Goldberg Var. 16) take sharp dotting; elsewhere in Bach decide case by case, and line up dotted figures with other voices.

topics.title: Lombard rhythm
topics.summary: Short–long figures (the "Lombard snap") are played with the first note as short as possible.

rules.text: The short note before the long one is played faster than written.

guidelines.text: The shorter the first note, the livelier and bolder the effect; but do not hurry, or it sounds like common dance music.

topics.title: Unequal quick notes (inégales)
topics.summary: Quantz asks for a slight lengthening of the "good" notes among the quickest values in moderate and slow pieces. The modern Bach authors are cautious about applying this to Bach.

rules.text: Applies to the quickest notes of a moderate or slow piece: crotchets in 3/2, quavers in 3/4 and ¢, semiquavers in 3/8, semiquavers or demisemiquavers in 2/4 and common time.
The 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th notes are held slightly longer and played slightly stronger; never as much as dotted.
Exceptions: very fast passage-work; vocal coloratura; notes with strokes or dots; repeated notes; slurs over more than two notes; gigue quavers.

guidelines.text: Bodky sets French inégalité aside for Bach until better evidence appears.
Badura-Skoda treats Quantz's inequality as a "mini-rubato" of emphasis, not a stammering long–short.
On flute the single tongue makes quick notes too even; tiri and did'll produce the slight inequality naturally.

checks: Q XI read in full; exception list matches BS p. 69.

topics.title: Dotted notes against triplets
topics.summary: When one part has triplets and another a dotted figure, Quantz and C. P. E. Bach give opposite answers.

rules.text: Quantz: play the short note after the third triplet note, not with it, or it sounds like 6/8.
C. P. E. Bach: dotted figures and duplets against triplets are assimilated to the triplet.

guidelines.text: Mitchell cites the E minor Partita Gavotte and the E minor fugue of WTC II for the assimilating practice; decide by the style of the piece.

checks: Disagreement listed in Reilly's note to Q V §22.

topics.title: Rests, syncopations and keeping time
topics.summary: Short rests, syncopations and slow notes inside fast passages are where players most often lose the beat.

rules.text: After a short rest on the beat, enter late: wait about half as long again as the rest, then make the next note shorter.
Keep the tempo at every crotchet, not just at the start and end of the bar.
On flute, move the fingers with the withdrawal of the tongue, not before it, or passages rush.

guidelines.text: Hold the first note of quick figures slightly to stop ascending passages from rushing.
Play triplets round and even; hold the first a fraction rather than rushing the first two.
Syncopations should sound as displaced downbeats, not glued to the beat.

topics.title: Tempo rubato over a steady beat
topics.summary: Eighteenth-century rubato is a melody that moves freely against an accompaniment that keeps strict time.

rules.text: One hand (or the soloist) plays against the bar; the other (or the accompanist) keeps strict time; they meet together over the bass at the end.
The accompanist must not follow or hurry when the soloist delays or anticipates notes.

guidelines.text: Rubato suits slow, caressing or sad melodies and dissonant chords; avoid frequent ritardandos in affettuoso music.
Italian Concerto, Andante: a written-out Italian rubato; on harpsichord a note played a shade early sounds longer and more singing.
A solo keyboardist may vary the bass but not the harmony.

topics.title: Flute tonguing: ti, di, tiri, did'll
topics.summary: For Quantz the tongue does for the flute what the bow does for the violin. Three kinds of articulation, with many shades between a firm and a gentle stroke.

rules.text: ti: short, equal, lively or quick notes; leaps in an Allegro; notes with strokes; dotted notes even in an Adagio.
di: slow, sustained, pleasing notes; stepwise motion; always in the Adagio except dotted notes.
Under a slur, tongue only the first note (usually with di).
tiri: dotted notes and moderately quick passages. The accent is on ri (long, on the strong note), ti short on the weak; begin with ti ti.
did'll (double tongue): only for the quickest passage-work; accent on the first syllable, on the good note.

guidelines.text: The sound comes from the air released when the tongue tip withdraws, not from striking; move the stroke forward on the palate as you rise in pitch.
Leave a tiny separation before an appoggiatura so it is heard clearly.
Repeated notes under a slur are "huffed" from the chest; with dots too, more sharply.
Faster than tiri allows: slur pairs (ti ri ti ti pattern) so the tongue rests.
Bowing analogue: ti ≈ a short separate stroke; di ≈ a gentle stroke on the string; a slur is one bow (L. Mozart).

topics.title: Where to breathe (flute)
topics.summary: Breath is phrasing: breathing in the wrong place is like a breath in the middle of a word.

rules.text: Breathe between a long note and a short one; never after a short note, still less after the last note of a bar.
Exception: in quick stepwise triplets you may breathe after the bar's last note; with a leap of a third, breathe inside the leap.
Before a restated theme or a new idea (also after a cadence), breathe to separate the ideas.
Tied notes: split a tied quaver into two semiquavers on the same pitch and breathe between them.
A solo cadenza for wind instrument or voice must fit in one breath.

guidelines.text: In a bar of semiquavers the best breath is after the first note of a group, preferably where the notes leap.
If forced to breathe in quick notes: make the note before the breath very short and catch up over the next few notes so the beat does not slow.
Breathe in good time and only when needed; in public you will need more breaths than when practising alone.
At a rest, hold the last note slightly rather than leaving it at once.
Bowing analogue: L. Mozart wants many notes in one stroke and a break only where the phrase's incisions demand it, mocking the singer who breathes after every short phrase.
Keyboard analogue: wind solo works show breathing pauses most plainly, but every line needs them (see Keyboard "breathing").

topics.title: Keyboard touch: detached, legato, ordinary
topics.summary: C. P. E. Bach gives the norms; Badura-Skoda and Bodky test them on Bach.

rules.text: Notes with strokes or dots are held a little less than half their written length.
Notes under a slur are held for their full length; in slurred groups of 2 or 4, slightly more pressure on the 1st and 3rd; in groups of 3, on the first.
Passing notes and appoggiaturas against the bass are played legato even without a slur.
The first note of a slur is slightly accented; when a slur ends, the last note is released.

guidelines.text: In general Allegros take detached notes and Adagios broad slurred ones, but every kind of touch occurs in every tempo.
Avoid both "sticky" holding and leaving the keys "as if they burned".
Unmarked notes "are held for half their value" is C. P. E. Bach's ordinary touch; Badura-Skoda calls this an extreme and prefers a slight shortening.
Bodky's rule of thumb: Allegro → non-legato to staccato; Adagio → legato; Moderato → steps (and often thirds) slurred, larger leaps detached.
Walking basses: slightly detached like a cellist, not choppy; the faster the tempo, the shorter.
Figura corta: legato in a gentle Adagio; detached and energetic in quick tempos.
Legato technique: release one finger as the next strikes; in an "articulated legato" release just before, letting the string resonance bridge.

topics.title: Keyboard "breathing": phrasing pauses
topics.summary: A keyboard needs no air, but its lines still need breaths. Badura-Skoda asks teachers to mark breathing in every voice, the way a string quartet marks bowings.

guidelines.text: "Even the strongest lungs have to breathe somewhere": breathing pauses sit between the pillars of a steady beat.
On harpsichord, unstressed notes can only be made shorter (timing, articulation), since finger pressure gives no dynamics.
No articulation, or the same articulation everywhere, is like text with no punctuation.

steps: Sing the line, as C. P. E. Bach advises, and mark where a singer or flautist would breathe (Quantz's rules).
Turn each breath into a small lift taken from the end of the note before it, not a delay of the next beat.
Mark the metrical weight: in 4/4 beats 1 and 3 strong (3 less), 2 and 4 weak; in triple time the first beat strongest. Show it by weight and length.
Map L. Mozart's bowing: a down-bow downbeat = weight into the key; an up-bow upbeat = lighter, often after a lift.
Mark breaths independently in each voice of polyphony so the entries can be heard.

crossRefs.point: First note of the bar down-bow; upbeat and last note of the bar up-bow.
crossRefs.analogue: Keyboard: weight on the downbeat, lift before it. Flute: firm tongue on the strong note, breathe before the upbeat, not after it.

crossRefs.point: Every tone, even the strongest, starts and ends with a little softness.
crossRefs.analogue: Flute: begin with the tongue, not a push of air. Keyboard: release cleanly, never a thump.

crossRefs.point: Slurred pairs: first louder and a little longer, second quietly and slightly late.
crossRefs.analogue: CPE's pressure on the first of a slur; Quantz's ti–di pairing.

topics.title: Appoggiaturas
topics.summary: Appoggiaturas turn consonances into dissonances that resolve, binding the melody together. All three primary sources agree on the core proportions.

rules.text: The small note takes its time from the FOLLOWING note; the previous note is never shortened (C. P. E. Bach).
Before a plain note: half its value.
Before a dotted note: two thirds; the main note keeps only the dot.
Quantz: in 6/8 and 6/4 with a dotted note tied to the next, the appoggiatura takes the whole first dotted note.
Before a trill on a dissonance (aug. 4th, dim. 5th, 7th, 2nd) the appoggiatura is very short, so the dissonance is not turned into a consonance.
The appoggiatura is louder than its resolution and joined to it; the resolution is light.
Taken from the side of the preceding note: from above if that note is higher, from below if lower.

guidelines.text: Quantz: before a note followed by a rest the appoggiatura takes the note's value and the note takes the rest's (unless you need the breath).
Short (invariable) appoggiaturas: before quick notes, repeated notes, syncopations, triplets; ones that fill in falling thirds.
Add unmarked appoggiaturas where a long consonant note follows short ones.
Swell the appoggiatura if time allows and slur the resolution more softly (the Abzug).
Lengthen for affect; shorten if the accompaniment would make fifths or harsh sevenths. Never spoil the voice leading.
L. Mozart: never separate the appoggiatura from its note: one bow (flute: one tongue stroke; keyboard: legato into the resolution).

topics.title: Trills (shakes)
topics.summary: Trills begin from the upper note or an appoggiatura, keep an even speed, and usually end with a termination.

rules.text: A trill alternates the note with its upper second, a whole or half step as the key requires; never a trill in thirds.
C. P. E. Bach: the normal trill always starts on the upper note.
Quantz: every shake starts with its appoggiatura (from above or below) and ends with a two-note termination at the same speed; if only "tr" is written, both are implied.
The appoggiatura is tongued; shake and termination are slurred to it (flute).
A trill must be even; never faster than you can play evenly.

guidelines.text: Quantz's speed: a long cadential trill ≈ four finger movements (eight notes) per pulse (≈80/min); quicker in gay pieces, slower in sad ones and low registers.
Slower in a resonant hall, quicker in a small or carpeted room.
C. P. E. Bach prefers a rapid trill, broadened slightly in sad pieces; the trill lasts the whole note (except short trills).
No suffix in descending chains of trills, on short notes or triplets, or when the following notes already supply it.
Pralltriller (short trill): only on a falling second, joined to the previous note, snapped.
Avoid trills on augmented seconds and trills that create forbidden fifths.
L. Mozart lists four speeds: slow (sad pieces), medium, rapid, and accelerating (cadenzas).

topics.title: Small graces: mordent, turn, half-shake, battement
topics.summary: Quantz groups these French "brilliants" with the appoggiatura: plain appoggiaturas express tenderness, the brilliants gaiety.

rules.text: Half-shakes may replace the plain Abzug on upper appoggiaturas; pincés (mordents) and doublés (turns) go with lower appoggiaturas.
Battements may be used on leaps, where appoggiaturas are not allowed.

guidelines.text: In descending passage-work, half-shakes on the 1st or 3rd notes; in ascending passages, battements — sparingly.

flags: C. P. E. Bach's chapters on the turn and mordent were not read in detail; specific CPE rules are not included.

topics.title: How much to ornament
topics.summary: Every source warns against over-ornamenting: ornaments are seasoning, not the meal.

rules.text: Ornaments must never contradict the prevailing sentiment of the melody.
Ornament tones follow the key signature and any modulation.

guidelines.text: Use embellishments sparingly, especially in quick passages.
Vary ornaments on repeats (caressing, then brilliant, or plain).
French composers write their ornaments; in Italian Adagios the player adds them. Learn the French manner first.
Play a lesson first without ornaments, then with them.
Thorough-bass knowledge is needed to ornament well.

topics.title: Cadenzas and fermatas
topics.summary: A cadenza is made on the penultimate bass note (the dominant) at a fermata. Short, surprising, and grown from the piece itself.

rules.text: A cadenza for a wind instrument or voice must fit in one breath; a string player may be longer.
A short cadenza stays in the key; a longer one goes naturally to the subdominant; a still longer one to the subdominant and the dominant. No remote keys.
Dissonances in a cadenza are prepared and resolved correctly.
Two-part cadenzas follow the rules of composition and imitation, and may be a little longer.

guidelines.text: Take the principal sentiment and, if you like, repeat or imitate the most pleasing phrase of the piece.
Short and fresh "like a bon mot"; it must sound improvised; avoid regular metre.
Unmeasured, like an improvisation, with pauses between statements like conversation.

topics.title: Light and shade: principles
topics.summary: Forte and piano alternate constantly; the music itself tells you where.

rules.text: In general dissonances are played louder and consonances softer.
Notes outside the key (raised by sharps or naturals) are stressed; notes within the key softer.
Deceptive progressions and unexpected turns are brought out.

guidelines.text: Repetitions and sequences can go forte then piano.
A long note that interrupts quick notes gets particular emphasis; deep notes in leaps are played stronger.
Avoid constant changes of level.
L. Mozart: a minim among short notes is accented and then relaxed; notes tied over the barline get no accent at the barline.

topics.title: Dissonance dynamics (Quantz)
topics.summary: For the keyboard accompanist Quantz grades the dissonances into three classes of loudness. C. P. E. Bach accepted the principle only broadly.

rules.text: Consonant chords in a solo Adagio: mezzo piano, leaving room above and below.
Mezzo forte: 4/2, 6/5, 6 with minor 3rd, minor 7th with minor 3rd, major 7th.
Forte: 4♯/2 (second with augmented fourth), diminished 5th with minor 6th.
Fortissimo: ♯2/♯4, minor 3rd with augmented 4th, diminished 5th with major 6th, augmented 6th, diminished 7th, 7/4/2.
In piano or pianissimo passages, scale the classes down (pp: the strongest gets only mf).

guidelines.text: 9ths, 9/4, 9/7, 5/4, and a 7th over a passing note need no special emphasis.
Close spacing makes dissonances harsher than wide spacing.

Harpsichord means: piano = lighter touch and fewer parts; mf = bass in octaves; f = also chord tones in the left hand; ff = also quick arpeggios from below and a firmer touch; a second manual gives pp.

flags: The OCR of the mf list is ambiguous ("major sixth with minor third"); check against the printed table (Tab. XXIV).

topics.title: Swelling a long note (messa di voce)
topics.summary: On a long note in an Adagio the flute swells and diminishes; the keyboard must find substitutes.

rules.text: Tip the note gently, begin pianissimo, swell to the middle and diminish to the end; a finger vibrato (flattement) on the nearest open hole may be added.
Keep the pitch steady while swelling and diminishing (turn the flute in or out as needed).

guidelines.text: Bowing analogue: L. Mozart's first division of the bow (soft–loud–soft) is the same shape; a singer sustaining a long note without breathing.
Keyboard substitutes: on harpsichord, broken chords, trills and mordents sustain a long note; on clavichord, Bebung (vibrato) after half the note and portato.
Use the flattement sparingly; it is an ornament, not a continuous vibrato.

topics.title: Dynamics on harpsichord, clavichord and piano
topics.summary: Each keyboard makes loud and soft differently. Bodky and Badura-Skoda read Bach's own manual markings as the model.

rules.text: On a two-manual harpsichord, change manuals for whole passages, not for small shadings.

guidelines.text: Harpsichord: terrace dynamics. Dances usually one colour; large works two or three levels (single, octave-doubled, full), changed after rests or fermatas.
Bach's models: Italian Concerto (tutti/solo on forte and piano manuals), French Overture (fugal sections forte, episodes piano), Goldberg (manual indications).
Clavichord: range about ppp–mf; intimate, "a lyric poem read to oneself"; don't overuse Bebung.
Contrasting themes should not be rattled off at one level.

topics.title: The one-keyed flute: practical points
topics.summary: Points from Quantz that are specific to the baroque flute and still useful on a modern one.

rules.text: Semitone trills: moderate the breath and strike the finger close to the hole so the upper note does not become a whole tone.

guidelines.text: Low notes in leaps need more strength: they cut less than high notes.
Raise all fingers equally and not too high; tongue and fingers together.
Quantz's trill fingerings (Tab. VII) are for the one-keyed flute; on a Boehm flute use modern trill fingerings but keep the principle of true intonation.

flags: Individual trill fingerings were not transcribed (they are for the one-keyed flute).

topics.title: Harpsichord, clavichord or piano
topics.summary: C. P. E. Bach wanted players to own both harpsichord and clavichord; the modern authors accept the piano for Bach with care.

rules.text: Harpsichord for ensembles; clavichord for solo playing and for judging a player; the pianoforte, if well made, fine alone and in small ensembles.

guidelines.text: Practise on both: clavichord for expressive touch, harpsichord for strength; harpsichord-only players play in one colour.
Quantz thought the pianoforte the best accompanying keyboard, the clavichord lacking only the fortissimo.
Piano for Bach: avoid dynamic extremes and "Busoni basses"; use the pedal discreetly to imitate harpsichord resonance, never long pedals.
Don't imitate the harpsichord on the piano, or the piano on the harpsichord.
Some WTC pieces suit the house organ (long sustained notes); decide the instrument piece by piece.
Temperament: take a barely noticeable amount from most fifths so all keys are usable.

topics.title: The keyboard as timekeeper
topics.summary: C. P. E. Bach calls the keyboard the guardian of the beat in ensemble music.

rules.text: Place the keyboard in the centre, with the first violinist near it; it keeps the time and makes small tempo changes possible.

guidelines.text: Repeat sustained chords to mark the metre in ensemble.
Fast repeated bass notes with another bass instrument: C. P. E. Bach omits some and plays the rest in octaves; Quantz wants every note.

checks: Disagreement noted by Mitchell (CPE p. 33 n.).

topics.title: Accompanying a soloist
topics.summary: What the accompanist does while the soloist plays freely.

rules.text: Keep strict time under the soloist's rubato; do not follow delays or anticipations.
Strengthen the tone where the subject enters and on dissonances.

guidelines.text: Moderate the forte; light short strokes in merry passages, long simple strokes in sad ones (L. Mozart for strings; on keyboard, touch and number of parts).
Watch the soloist and each other.

topics.title: Where the sources disagree
topics.summary: The same court (Berlin), the same decade, and still different answers. Show the positions side by side; let the player choose by style.

tables.title: Points of disagreement
rows: Before the beat, in the previous note's time (French coulé) — VIII, pp. 93–94
On the beat, short; the "unaccented" kind is "repulsive" — II.2, pp. 97–98
Some examples agree with Quantz (cited by Reilly, Q p. 93 n.)
With its appoggiatura, from above or below — IX, p. 103
Always from the upper note — II.3, p. 100
Upper note, or a longer appoggiatura, or from below — X, pp. 186–202
Appoggiatura before the closing note after a cadential trill
Allowed — II.2 (cited Reilly, Q p. 108 n.)
Even and moderate; ≈ 8 notes per pulse
Rapid preferred; slightly broader in sad pieces
Short note after the third triplet note — V §22
Three graded classes (mf, f, ff) — XVII.vi, p. 256
Dissonances louder in general; the graded scheme accepted only broadly
Repeated quick bass notes in continuo
Slight inequality of good notes — XI §12
Bodky: set aside; Badura-Skoda: only a "mini-rubato"
Berlin adagios slower, allegros faster than elsewhere

checks: Each cell traced to the cited section; L. Mozart cells marked cross-ref.

app-plain.title: Accented appoggiatura on a plain note
app-plain.caption: The small F takes half of the E (a 4th resolving to a 3rd over C). Louder appoggiatura, softer resolution, slurred.

app-dotted.title: Appoggiatura before a dotted note
app-dotted.caption: Before a dotted note the appoggiatura takes two thirds; the main note keeps only the value of the dot.

app-rest.title: Appoggiatura before a note followed by a rest (Quantz)
app-rest.caption: The appoggiatura takes the note's time and the note takes the rest's time, unless you need the rest to breathe.

app-passing.title: Falling thirds with small notes: Quantz vs C. P. E. Bach
app-passing.caption: Quantz (French coulé): the small notes are tipped BEFORE the beat, in the time of the previous note. C. P. E. Bach rejects this and puts them short ON the beat.

app-before-dissonant-trill.title: Short appoggiatura before a trill on a dissonance
app-before-dissonant-trill.caption: Over B in the bass, the trilled F is a diminished 5th. A long G would turn it into a 6th, a consonance, so the appoggiatura is very short.
app-before-dissonant-trill.note: Example chosen by the pack author (Quantz's own figures are not transcribed). Speed: eight notes per pulse at crotchet ≈ 80 (Q IX, p. 102).

trill-cadential-q.title: Cadential trill (Quantz)
trill-cadential-q.caption: Begins with its appoggiatura (here from above, held half the note), ends with a two-note termination at trill speed. No appoggiatura between the termination and the closing note.

trill-cpe.title: Trill from the upper note with suffix (C. P. E. Bach)
trill-cpe.caption: Every normal trill starts on the upper note; rapid rather than slow; the suffix (two notes from below) joins it to the next note.

pralltriller.title: Short trill (Pralltriller) on a falling second
pralltriller.caption: Only on a descending second, joined to the previous note; upper tone snapped at the end.

overdot.title: Dotted quavers: the short note is played shorter
overdot.caption: The note after the dot is as short as the shortest note in the piece, whatever the tempo; the dot is held longer.

lombard.title: Lombard rhythm (short–long)
lombard.caption: The first note is as short as possible; the shorter it is, the bolder the effect.

inequality.title: Slight inequality of the quickest notes (Quantz)
inequality.caption: In moderate and slow pieces the "good" notes (1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th) are held a little longer and played a little stronger, but much less than dotted.
inequality.note: The 0.29/0.21 split is the pack author's illustration of "slightly"; Quantz gives no ratio.

dot-vs-triplet.title: Dotted figure against triplets
dot-vs-triplet.caption: Quantz: the short note comes after the third triplet note. C. P. E. Bach: assimilate it to the triplet.

rest-delay.title: Short rest on the beat (Quantz)
rest-delay.caption: Wait about half as long again as the rest seems to last; the following note is then shorter.

breath-q.title: Where to breathe in a semiquaver passage (flute)
breath-q.caption: Breathe between a long note and a short one, never after a short note or the last note of a bar. If you must breathe inside running semiquavers, do it after the first note of a group, where the notes leap; shorten that note and catch up so the beat does not slow.

breaths.why: long → short: the best breath, taken before the passage-work starts
only if needed: after the first note of a group, inside the leap G4→B4

tongue-q.title: Tonguing syllables (Quantz)
tongue-q.caption: ti for short lively notes and leaps; di for slow and stepwise notes; tiri for dotted notes (ri on the strong note, start ti ti); did'll for the quickest passage-work.

bow-map.title: One passage, three instruments (L. Mozart cross-reference)
bow-map.caption: Down-bow on the first of the bar, up-bow on the upbeat (L. Mozart) ↔ firm "ti"/weight on the strong note and a lighter "di" on the weak one (Quantz) ↔ keyboard: weight into the downbeat, lift (a "breath") before the upbeat.
bow-map.note: Mozart's upbeat rule: the upbeat note is taken up-bow, the bar's first note down-bow.

diss-dyn.title: Dissonance dynamics on the harpsichord (Quantz)
diss-dyn.caption: Consonant chords mezzo piano with few parts; louder dissonances use more parts, bass in octaves and finally a quick arpeggio. The labels are Quantz's three classes.

performed.rule: consonant: 3 upper parts, light touch | mf: + bass doubled at the lower octave | f: + extra chord tones in the left hand | ff: as f, quick arpeggio from below, firmer touch

tools.title: Quantz tempo calculator
tools.spec: Inputs: metre (C, ¢, 2/4, 3/4, 3/8, 6/8, 9/8, 12/8), tempo word (dropdown grouped by Quantz class + plain Allegro), fastest note value, optional pulse (default 80, slider 60–100). Output: MM for the counting unit, the pulse placement (text + a bar diagram with dots where pulses fall), the Quantz class, and Bodky's nearest group for comparison. "Tap pulse" button measures the user's own pulse/tempo by taps. Play: harpsichord click on pulses plus a soft tick on the counting unit for 2 bars.
tools.reference: quantz-pulse tables quantz-classes and quantz-triple; bodky-groups

tools.title: Appoggiatura length lab
tools.spec: Pick a case (plain note, dotted note, 6/8 tied, before a rest, before a trill on a dissonance, falling thirds) and a source (Quantz / C. P. E. Bach / L. Mozart where given). Shows written vs performed in two staves, highlights the dissonance against the bass, and plays both (harpsichord). When the sources disagree (falling thirds), show both realisations with a toggle.

tools.title: Rhythm lab: dots, Lombard, inequality, triplets
tools.spec: One short passage per mode. Dotted: slider from written (3:1) to sharp (7:1) and "as short as the shortest note". Lombard: slider for the first note. Inequality: slider 50:50 → 60:40 with a "Quantz exceptions" checklist that disables it (strokes, repeated notes, long slurs, very fast, gigue). Triplets: toggle Quantz vs C. P. E. Bach. Always plays written and altered versions back to back.

tools.title: Trill builder
tools.spec: Choose: start (upper note / appoggiatura from above held half the note / from below), speed (notes per pulse, default Quantz 8 at pulse 80; register adjustment), termination on/off, short trill (Pralltriller). Presets: Quantz cadential, C. P. E. Bach normal, CPE Pralltriller, L. Mozart accelerating. Shows the realised notes and plays them. Warn when the user sets a long appoggiatura before a trill on a dissonance.

tools.title: Breath & articulation planner
tools.spec: Input: a melody in the mini-notation (or pick a stored example). Flute mode: marks candidate breaths by Quantz VII (long→short, not after a bar's last note, before a new idea, at leaps in semiquavers, split ties) with a reason for each, and proposes syllables (ti/di/tiri/did'll) by note value, step/leap and tempo class. Keyboard mode: the same breaths become lifts (shown as commas), metrical weight shown (strong/weak), and an optional "bowing view" showing L. Mozart down/up bows as a cross-reference. All marks are editable by the user; the tool labels them as suggestions.
tools.reference: breathing, tonguing, keyboard-breathing; examples breath-q, tongue-q, bow-map

tools.title: Dissonance dynamics
tools.spec: Input a bass note + figures (or pick the example progression). Output Quantz's class (consonant / mf / f / ff), scaled by a global level (pp/p/mp). Harpsichord playback realises the class by texture (number of parts, octave bass, arpeggio) since a harpsichord cannot change dynamic by touch; a piano option uses velocity.

tools.title: Messa di voce & bow divisions
tools.spec: Visual only (no harpsichord audio): a long note drawn as a dynamic envelope. Presets: Quantz messa di voce (pp→swell to middle→diminish), L. Mozart's four bow divisions (cross-ref), and keyboard substitutes (harpsichord: trill/broken chord filling; clavichord: Bebung after half the note) shown as note patterns that can be played.
